crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: AI and Authorship
children.blurb: AI and authorship examines how generative systems change who or what can be credited as an author, covering human-AI collaboration, disclosure norms, originality, and the integrity of scholarly and creative records.

children.name: Fabricated Citations and Fact Checking
children.blurb: Fabricated citations are references in AI papers that point to nonexistent works, or to real works with wrong authors, titles, or venues.

children.name: Training Data and Academic Work
children.blurb: This topic covers the use of scholarly texts, including journal articles, preprints, theses, textbooks and course materials, as training data for machine learning systems.

children.name: Ethics Review with AI Assistance
children.blurb: AI assistance in ethics review means using machine learning tools to help research ethics committees and institutional review boards screen protocols, identify risks, check consent forms, and flag missing safeguards.

children.name: Provenance of Research Images and Data
children.blurb: Provenance of research images and data concerns the documented origin, processing history, and chain of custody for visual and tabular evidence used in scientific work.

sections.body: This field is about how artificial intelligence changes the way research is produced, checked, and trusted. It covers questions of who gets credit when a model helps write a paper, how to catch citations that do not exist, where training data comes from, how ethics boards can use AI without losing human judgment, and how to trace images and datasets back to their source. In practice, AI is now drafting sections of manuscripts, summarizing literature, generating code, and producing or altering figures. It is also being used to screen submissions for plagiarism, image duplication, and statistical red flags. The work here is not about whether AI should exist in research, but about what happens to honesty and accountability when it does.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The state of this work is uneven. Authorship rules are still unsettled because most journals and funders say a model cannot be an author, but they do not always agree on how to disclose substantial AI assistance. Fact checking tools can catch some fabricated citations, especially when a reference has a DOI or page range that does not match any real article, but they miss subtler hallucinations that sound plausible. Training data provenance is a weak point, since many large models are built on corpora whose full contents are not public, and academic work scraped from the web may include copyrighted or personal material. Ethics review with AI assistance is mostly experimental, with tools that can help draft protocols or spot missing risk categories, but no system is trusted to make the final judgment. Provenance of research images and data is improving through metadata standards and duplication detectors, yet manipulated figures can still pass if the manipulation is small or the original file is gone. The honest limit is that these tools reduce some errors, but they do not replace a careful reader.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The five pages under this section move from the person to the evidence. AI and Authorship is the starting point for questions about credit, disclosure, and responsibility when a model contributes to a paper. Fabricated Citations and Fact Checking then looks at the output itself, showing how false references appear and what checking methods can and cannot do. Training Data and Academic Work goes one step back to the inputs, asking where the text and code used to train models actually come from and what that means for scholarly work. Ethics Review with AI Assistance shifts to the institutional process, covering how review boards might use these tools while keeping human oversight. Provenance of Research Images and Data closes the loop by focusing on the raw materials of evidence, from microscopy images to spreadsheets, and how to record their history. A reader who wants to understand a single paper's integrity might start with the first two pages, while someone building a lab policy would move through all five in order. The site's library of 135 research papers sits behind these pages, and each link goes to the original paper rather than a secondary search tool.
